pr_title: Support ADD COLUMN, ALTER PRIMARY KEY, DROP COLUMN in one stmt
pr_body:
This PR laid out foundations to support DDL stmt that requires constructing more than one primary index. In particular, this work is centered around supporting ADD COLUMN(s), ALTER PRIMARY KEY, DROP COLUMN(s) in one ALTER TABLE statement, which would require constructing at least one, and at most three primary indexes to achieve a correct online schema change.

The general idea to achieve this is to construct a sequence of four primary indexes, each sourced from the previous one, `old` <-- `inter1` <-- `inter2` <-- `final`, where
 - `old` is the existing, public primary indexes;
 - `inter1` is the one that includes all the to-be-added and to-be-dropped columns;
 - `inter2` has the same columns as `inter1` but has its key columns altered (to handle the ALTER PRIMARY KEY command)
 - `final` is the final primary index with the correct set of columns and correct key after completing the schema change.

For each ALTER TABLE stmt, if we determined that new primary index is needed, we initialize this sequence of primary indexes by cloning from `old` (this action is also known as "inflating a chain of primary indexes"). Once we have all four primary indexes, we process each ADD COLUMN, ALTER PRIMARY KEY, and DROP COLUMN command by modifying some of the primary indexes:
 - ADD COLUMN: add the column as a stored column to `inter1`, `inter2`, and `final`;
 - ALTER PRIMARY KEY: alter the key/stored columns in `inter2` and `final`;
 - DROP COLUMN: drop the column from stored columns from `final`.

At the end of the statement building, we run a post-processing step on the chain to eliminate redundant primary indexes. E.g. ALTER TABLE DROP COLUMN will only modify `final`, so `old`, `inter1`, `inter2` will have the same columns and thus we can remove `inter1` and `inter2`. The final primary index transition will then be `old` <-- `final`.

Fixes https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/issues/99035
Epic: None
Release note: None
pr_comments: This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/cockroachdb/cockroach/99526)

This should be ready for a look. I recognized that it is a big PR but I don't see an easy way to break it apart further. It is a major overhaul in the builder of several stmts (ADD COLUMN, DROP COLUMN, and ALTER PK). I think the easiest way to start reviewing is to understand the general approach as described in the PR first, and look for how it's exactly being implemented second in the code.

Thanks in advance.

I like the goal of this PR very much. I don't think I'll have any objections of principle. I have a few comments before proceeding any further:
1. Can you spin off commits 1, 2 and 4 into a separate PR which can be merged quickly? Those changes are quite uncontroversial and I don't expect anything but nits 
2. Looking at commit 3, the one introducing `EXPLAIN (DDL, PK)`: I tried it out in a `cockroach demo` session after running the example in your release notes and all I'm seeing is a bunch of numbers: `Table 104: [1 : 2, 3]  <--  [1 : 2, 3, 4]  <--  [2 : 1, 3, 4]  <--  [2 : 1, 4]`. Can we have table and index and column names in there? It shouldn't be hard to generate placeholder names for nameless things. Also, the `treeprinter` package is quite easy to use, this output could be multiline. Finally, it's worth thinking about expanding this beyond just PKs; isn't what we really want here to know how many backfills (and perhaps also validations) the schema change is going to trigger? This seems like something that would be very useful to users whereas this PK flag as it is is only useful for the purposes of testing this PR. I don't want this to hold up this PR however. What do you think?
4. I'm finding the last commit a bit hard to review due to the large amount of noise in the diffs of the test output. That's the name of the game with these kinds of PRs but it seems that a large amount of noise is due to index and constraint IDs being bumped to higher values. In this optimization step, which removes redundant indexes, could we also remap the IDs of the new elements to make them contiguous with the existing ones? Like, if the NextIndexID index ID of a table is 3 before doing a vanilla ADD COLUMN (like in the `add_column` integration test), then the new primary index should have index ID 3 instead of 6. Regardless of the ease of review it's also the case that IDs jumping forward like this can be cause for confusion when trying to interpret an `EXPLAIN (DDL)` in production.
5. Following up on my previous question, would it be worth doing this optimization at pre-commit time instead? I'm very willing to believe that the answer to this question may in fact be "no" but it's something I was wondering about when implementing the generalized statement-time execution.

@postamar 
1. yes, those commits are now in this [PR](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/pull/103476).
2. Completely agreed! The initial purpose of me adding this additional EXPLAIN flag is to help me develop/debug this PR. I definitely liked your idea of extending it to include important stages (like BACKFILL and VALIDATE) with pretty table/index/column names. I think we can put all these into a separate, observability-improving PR.
3. 4. Let's chat tomorrow in our 1:1

@postamar Can I have some early review feedback for the latest push?

Per our discussion, the latest change has made an effort to keep the indexID same as before for "vanilla" ALTER TABLE cases (i.e. cases where we only add a column, or drop a column, or alter a PK and thus only one new primary index is created). 
The approach I used is to give "placeholder"/"temporary" IDs to newly added, possibly redundant primary indexes, and during post-processing, after we remove redundant primary indexes, we re-assign actual, sensible IDs to them. 

This has decreased some 100+ test file diffs and now it's some 300+ file diffs. I think we can leverage your `EXPLAIN(DDL, SHAPE)` and focus the test diff there. Those diffs are expected to me and I've noted some comments there too to help understand the diff. Hopefully, this effort helps you review this big PR.

Also, if you have any other suggestions to make the review easier, feel free to let me know!
Will do ASAP! Very excited about this.

TFTR!

CI is flaky so I am going to merge it...

bors r+

issue_context.title: schemachanger: Support ADD COLUMN, ALTER PRIMARY KEY, DROP COLUMN in one ALTER TABLE stmt
issue_context.body:
With the recent development in the declarative schema changer, we are now ready to support add column, alter primary key, drop column in one alter table statement. For example,
```
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN i, ALTER PRIMARY KEY USING COLUMNS (i), DROP COLUMN j, DROP COLUMN k, ADD COLUMN p
```

Jira issue: CRDB-25674


Epic CRDB-27601

review_comments: What happens if we don't fall back here?

I don't think it's right to expose the user to this assertion failure, instead we should transparently fall back to the legacy schema changer so that they can get on with their lives. As far as we developers are concerned we certainly want to be informed about this, if we can have this message end up in the logs somehow we can look out for it in splunk.

It might be worth leaving a comment here. Normally, we mark any state transition that results in irretrievable information loss as non-revertible. In this case, going to DELETE_ONLY means we miss out on any concurrent inserts and updates. Presumably this is OK because the temp schema's state transitions are so tightly bound to the backfilled index?
Why disallow it? It's a dumb thing for a user to do, of course, but shouldn't the declarative schema changer be able to handle this gracefully without any extra code needed?

Why do we need to version-gate this? We're not adding any new elements or anything like that. If it's just because of the rules then we should backport the rules to 23.1 to ensure that in mixed-version clusters we can have a 23.1 node perform the schema change (and potentially roll it back) after the statement txn commits just like a 23.2 node would.
